trials.name: Footprint-pooled placement head
trials.hypothesis: Change: for each brick type, max- and min-pool the conv features over that type's footprint, anchored at the top-left cell, then score with a small per-type MLP. Why: where a brick lands and whether it fills only target cells depends on every cell under the footprint (the max height and the target at that layer), which a 1x1 head at one cell sees poorly. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is not above about 0.15.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

WIDTH = 64
DEPTH = 2
HID = 32


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        layers, c_in = [], spec.in_channels
        for _ in range(DEPTH):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(c_in, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
            c_in = WIDTH
        self.body = nn.Sequential(*layers)
        self.fps = [(int(fp[0]), int(fp[1])) for fp in spec.footprints]
        self.heads = nn.ModuleList([
            nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(2 * WIDTH, HID, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(HID, 1, 1))
            for _ in self.fps])
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        outs = []
        for (dy, dx), head in zip(self.fps, self.heads):
            if dy == 1 and dx == 1:
                mx, mn = f, f
            else:
                p = F.pad(f, (0, dx - 1, 0, dy - 1))
                mx = F.max_pool2d(p, (dy, dx), stride=1)
                mn = -F.max_pool2d(-p, (dy, dx), stride=1)
            outs.append(head(torch.cat([mx, mn], dim=1)))
        place = torch.cat(outs, dim=1).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)

trials.name: Footprint head, 2 PPO epochs
trials.hypothesis: Change: recipe only. Use r3c1 with ppo_epochs 2 instead of 4. The budget then gives about 180k samples and about 350 updates of 512 samples, instead of 97k samples and 190 updates. Why: the batch is already at its minimum, and more frequent updates on fresher data have helped every time so far. The total number of gradient steps stays about the same. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is below about 0.62, which would mean sample reuse mattered more.

trials.label: r4c3
trials.name: Footprint head, 64x8, lr 1e-3
trials.hypothesis: Change: recipe only. Use r3c1 with lr 1e-3 instead of 7e-4. Why: the linear decay to 0 means the average step is small, and with only about 190 updates a larger learning rate may give more improvement per update. The small batches have been stable so far, with r3c1's two seeds agreeing closely. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is below about 0.62 or the two seeds diverge strongly.

analyses.1: No trials yet. The baseline's 4 seeds are bimodal (0.068 ×3, 0.258 ×1), so seed luck dominates, and only a gain of more than about 0.1 in a 2-seed mean means much. This round is a 2x2 test: architecture change alone, recipe change alone, and both together. The architecture change targets the task directly. A brick at an anchor lands on the highest cell under its whole footprint, and the baseline scores it from a 1x1 head at one cell. Pooling learned features over each type's footprint before scoring should help the network learn where the brick lands and whether that spot is correct. The recipe change targets sample efficiency. The budget gives only about 32 updates of 4,096 samples, so smaller batches give more updates. The combined trial checks whether the two gains add up.
analyses.2: Round 1 tested two changes separately, then together (all values are 2-seed means). Smaller, more frequent updates alone (r1c2) left the baseline stuck at 0.068 on both seeds. That looks like a common failure mode: 0.068 is 35 of the 512 dev designs, and 3 of the baseline's 4 seeds landed exactly there. The footprint-pooled head alone (r1c1) got 0.10. The two together (r1c3) reached 0.36, but the seeds split widely (0.14 vs 0.58), so it may be less of a gain than it looks. The footprint head seems to help the agent escape the 0.068 mode, and more updates seem to help once the head is present. Training runs far below the time limit (86 of 900 s). Compute (FLOPs) is the real limit, so cheap changes are best. This round: (A) halve the batch again to give about twice as many updates; (B) add a cheap 1x1 per-column encoder so each cell can relate the build's height to the target's layers before spatial mixing; (C) add a new idea, feeding pooled whole-board context back into each cell's features before the footprint heads.
analyses.3: The footprint-pooled head is the main architectural gain. It scored 0.10 with the default recipe and 0.36 with 128 envs, and it is only useful when updates are small and frequent. Halving to 64 envs (r2c1) raised it to 0.59, with both seeds well above the baseline's 4-seed mean of 0.116. More frequent policy updates look like the strongest lever under this sample budget. Two network changes to the footprint head were tested only at 128 envs and both beat r1c3's 0.36 under the same recipe: the per-column 1x1 encoder (0.47, seeds 0.58 and 0.35) and the global context added to every cell (0.43, seeds 0.41 and 0.44). Both gains are within seed noise. This round makes one change each against r2c1: halve the rollout again to 64×8 for more updates, and move each of the two promising additions onto the 64-env recipe. That way their effects can be read cleanly before the final round.
analyses.4: The footprint-pooled head is the largest architectural gain, taking dev success from about 0.10 to 0.36 with the same recipe. Smaller and more frequent updates help steadily: 0.36 at 128x16, 0.59 at 64x16 and 0.70 at 64x8, where both seeds agree. The column encoder beat its no-encoder pair at both batch sizes (0.47 vs 0.36, then 0.645 vs 0.59) even with about 22% fewer samples, so it probably helps a little. Adding global context hurt twice (0.43 at 128 envs and 0.40 at 64 envs, both below their no-context pairs), so I drop it. 64 envs x 8 steps is the smallest batch allowed, so the only way left to get more updates is fewer PPO epochs, which buys more samples. In this last round I test three things on top of r3c1: adding the column encoder, using 2 epochs for about 1.85x more samples, and raising the learning rate.
